title: Newton's 3 Laws of Motion - The Physics Chalkboard

claims.text: Moving objects naturally keep moving; stopping requires an unbalanced force such as friction.
Acceleration is directly proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass (a = F/m).
Action and reaction force pairs always act on two different interacting objects and never cancel on a single body.

voice_performance.performance_intent: Clear, patient, highly engaging physics teacher guiding students through misconceptions with whiteboard reveals.
voice_performance.energy_curve: hooks with curiosity, builds methodical clarity through 3 laws, lands with punchy golden rule
voice_performance.pause_policy: 0.4s pause before revealing each law formula and misconception buster

sections.label: Hook & The Friction Trap
sections.text: Why does everything you think about motion feel completely backwards? If you slide a book across a table, it stops. But not because motion requires force. It stops because friction is an outside force fighting it!
sections.speaker_directions: Curious, conspiratorial teacher hook, emphatic delivery on 'backwards'

enhancement_cues.description: Chalkboard sketch of sliding book with opposing red friction vector arrow

sections.label: Law 1: Inertia
sections.text: That is Newton's First Law: Inertia. An object in motion stays in motion at a constant velocity, and an object at rest stays at rest, unless an unbalanced force acts on it. In deep space, with zero friction, you glide forever without burning any fuel.
sections.speaker_directions: Clear and pedagogical, pausing slightly after reciting the law definition

enhancement_cues.description: Deep space probe drifting silently with constant velocity vector arrow

sections.label: Law 2: F = ma
sections.text: So what happens when an unbalanced force does hit? Law Two: Force equals mass times acceleration! Acceleration is force divided by mass. Kick a soccer ball with 50 Newtons, and it flies. Kick a giant boulder with the same 50 Newtons, and its massive weight resists acceleration.
sections.speaker_directions: Energetic and comparative, highlighting the soccer ball vs boulder contrast

enhancement_cues.description: Side-by-side chalk balance: small mass = large acceleration arrow; huge mass = tiny arrow

sections.label: Law 3: Action & Reaction
sections.text: Now for the law everyone gets wrong: Action and Reaction. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. But here is the secret: they act on two different objects! When a rocket pushes exhaust gas down, the gas pushes the rocket up. They never cancel out because they act on different bodies.
sections.speaker_directions: Delighted teacher revealing the mystery trap that students always miss

enhancement_cues.description: Rocket launch chalkboard vector diagram showing opposite forces on rocket vs exhaust gas

sections.label: The Golden Rule
sections.text: Here is the golden rule to ace your physics exam: Forces do not cause motion. Unbalanced forces cause changes in motion!
sections.speaker_directions: Authoritative, crystallizing the main takeaway with punchy emphasis

enhancement_cues.description: Chalkboard callout card highlighting the core principle in bold yellow chalk

sections.label: Landing & Outro
sections.text: Next time you brake in a car and lurch forward, thank inertia. Subscribe and follow for more physics made simple!
sections.speaker_directions: Warm, conversational outro with friendly call to action
